definition: combine or unite into one
memoryTip: Dental amalgam mixes metals — amalgamate = blend into one.
correctPassage: The two small clinics will amalgamate next year into a single regional center.
wrongPassages: Managers hoped to amalgamate the budget deficit by spending even more on marketing.
She tried to amalgamate the argument by refusing to hear any opposing evidence.
The storm will amalgamate overnight as the cold front weakens and skies clear.

definition: formally announce or make widely known
memoryTip: Pro-mulgate: put the rule out so everyone hears it.
correctPassage: The agency will promulgate the new safety standards before the compliance deadline.
wrongPassages: They hoped to promulgate the surplus by quietly burying it in a locked warehouse.
The cleaner will promulgate the spill by pushing it under the nearest mat.
She tried to promulgate the rumor by refusing to speak about it to anyone.

definition: mutual exchange for mutual benefit
memoryTip: Reciprocal: you give, I give back — mutual benefit.
correctPassage: Trade negotiators insisted on reciprocity so each country would open its markets equally.
wrongPassages: Under a policy of reciprocity, only one side ever paid while the other kept taking.
She practiced reciprocity by accepting every favor and never returning any.
The treaty’s reciprocity clause required gifts to flow in one direction only.

definition: involve as a necessary consequence
memoryTip: En-tail: the decision drags consequences along behind it.
correctPassage: Accepting the fellowship will entail relocating for at least two years.
wrongPassages: The optional dessert did not entail any change to the meal plan or the bill.
His entail smile vanished the moment the first hard question was asked.
Choosing the free sample was said to entail nothing and change nothing at all.

definition: demand or specify as a condition of an agreement
memoryTip: Stipulate the terms — spell out conditions in the deal.
correctPassage: The contract stipulates that all research data remain public for five years.
wrongPassages: He tried to stipulate the error by deleting the logs so no one could check.
She hoped to stipulate the fever by ignoring the symptoms until morning.
The runner will stipulate failure by swallowing exceptions and reporting success.

definition: serving as a symbol of something
memoryTip: Like an emblem — stands for a bigger idea or era.
correctPassage: The abandoned mill became emblematic of the town’s industrial decline.
wrongPassages: Investors wanted emblematic markets where prices never moved more than a cent.
The blank page was called emblematic of a report packed with charts and findings.
Her thoroughly ordinary lunch order was somehow emblematic of radical innovation.

definition: a reduction or lessening
memoryTip: A-bate: turn down the volume — reduction (noise abatement).
correctPassage: Noise abatement measures cut late-night complaints from nearby residents.
wrongPassages: After the abatement of the storm, winds strengthened and flooding grew worse.
Tax abatement in this case meant every household owed a higher bill next year.
They celebrated the abatement of traffic by adding two more rush-hour lanes of congestion.

definition: lack of harmony; clash of sounds or ideas
memoryTip: Dis-sonance: harsh sound or clash — ideas that don’t fit.
correctPassage: Voters sensed dissonance between the campaign’s promises and its budget plan.
wrongPassages: The choir’s perfect unison was praised as pure dissonance from first note to last.
There was total dissonance among the panel: every member repeated the same conclusion.
She stored the dissonance in a drawer beside rubber bands and spare badges.

definition: reduce in extent or cut short
memoryTip: Cut the tail short — reduce or trim back.
correctPassage: Budget cuts will curtail after-school programs for the rest of the year.
wrongPassages: The board moved to curtail the program by doubling its staff and expanding hours.
They hoped to curtail the drought by seeding clouds and opening every reservoir.
Her curtail certificate claimed endless talks that had never been scheduled.

definition: courage and strength in pain or adversity
memoryTip: Fort + attitude — inner strength when things get hard.
correctPassage: Survivors showed remarkable fortitude during the long months of recovery.
wrongPassages: His fortitude collapsed at the first mild inconvenience of the day.
Reviewers called the methods fortitude once every step could be copied elsewhere.
She displayed fortitude by quitting the moment the problem required patience.

definition: serious, strict, and unrelenting
memoryTip: A stern face — no jokes, strict and unyielding.
correctPassage: The coach’s stern warning made clear that missed practices would not be excused.
wrongPassages: His stern laugh and easy shrug showed he was not taking the rule seriously.
She gave a stern endorsement of every loophole that weakened the policy.
Parents called the playground stern after children ran free with no rules at all.

definition: accurately predicting what will happen
memoryTip: Like a prophet — foresaw what later came true.
correctPassage: Her early essay now seems prophetic in light of the reforms that followed.
wrongPassages: His prophetic forecast missed every major trend of the next decade.
Critics called the edited version prophetic for erasing the song’s only distinctive edge.
A prophetic integration test mocks every dependency, including the system under test.

definition: publicly denounce or condemn
memoryTip: De-cry: cry out against something in public.
correctPassage: Local historians decry the demolition of the century-old theater.
wrongPassages: Sponsors moved to decry the festival by funding it and inviting every critic.
She decried the award by accepting it and praising the selection committee.
Parents decried the quiet concert after every child sat still for two peaceful hours.

definition: lack of seriousness; disrespectful levity
memoryTip: Flip answers — unserious jokes when gravity is needed.
correctPassage: Flippancy about lab safety rules has no place during hazardous experiments.
wrongPassages: Her flippancy showed in the careful, solemn tone she used throughout the eulogy.
The judge praised the witness’s flippancy for treating each question with full gravity.
She kept a spare flippancy in the desk drawer among rubber bands.

definition: having peculiar or unexpected traits
memoryTip: Full of quirks — oddly charming little peculiarities.
correctPassage: The café’s quirky menu pairs familiar dishes with unexpected spice blends.
wrongPassages: The completely standard office layout was praised as quirky for matching every other floor.
His quirky schedule never varied by a minute across ten identical workdays.
The approach felt quirky on a plain catwalk with ordinary welded railings.

definition: courtesy and mutual respect among people or nations
memoryTip: Comity ≈ committee of courtesy — polite mutual respect.
correctPassage: Diplomatic comity requires each government to treat the other’s envoys with respect.
wrongPassages: Comity collapsed into open insults the moment talks were televised live.
Under a spirit of comity, both sides refused every handshake and every courtesy.
The form field comity accepted any string and never validated it.

definition: bitingly sharp or critically caustic
memoryTip: Mord- = bite — mordant wit has a sharp bite.
correctPassage: Her mordant review left few illusions about the play’s weak second act.
wrongPassages: His mordant praise gushed with pure affection and no critical edge at all.
The trail was so mordant that first-time hikers finished early without maps.
She offered a mordant apology that carefully avoided any hint of sarcasm.

definition: involving a heavy burden or obligation
memoryTip: Onus = burden — an onerous task is crushingly heavy.
correctPassage: The reporting rules proved onerous for small nonprofits with tiny staffs.
wrongPassages: One click and a prefilled form made the process pleasantly onerous for everyone.
The clinic tried to onerous no-shows by double-booking every appointment slot.
Critics called the vacation policy onerous because it required almost no paperwork.

definition: a false appearance; a claim not based in fact
memoryTip: Pretend-sense — a fake show of something real.
correctPassage: Under the pretense of routine maintenance, the system was quietly redesigned.
wrongPassages: There was no pretense left once every claim had been verified with primary documents.
Her pretense of honesty meant she disclosed every conflict without hesitation.
The thermal fuse was pretense and never opened in the oven test.

definition: given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behavior
memoryTip: Like a goat’s caper — sudden leaps of mood or decision.
correctPassage: Capricious enforcement of the rules undermined any trust in the process.
wrongPassages: His capricious schedule never changed: same train, same desk, same lunch for years.
She treated the requirement as capricious after the client waived it in writing.
A capricious policy is one applied the same way to every case without exception.
